pedagogy.summary: Y4 extends the right-angle benchmark into naming and ordering: an acute angle is less open than a right angle, an obtuse angle is more open (up to a straight line, i.e. two right angles). Children classify angles as acute / right / obtuse and order them by openness. The persistent obstacle is comparing and ordering when arm lengths differ — the exact task where the arm-length misconception bites (Askew & Wiliam locate the most common error here). Naming should follow secure less-than / greater-than-a-right-angle comparison, not precede it.
bestPractices: Anchor both names to the right angle: acute = less open than a right angle, obtuse = more open (but less than a straight line); compare every angle to the checker before naming it.
Order by superimposing openings, not by eyeballing the tips: overlay angles vertex-on-vertex with one arm aligned so only the opening is compared — this defeats the arm-length and area traps.
Use a dynamic opening (hinge or fan) to sweep from acute through right to obtuse, naming each zone as it is passed.
Hunt for and colour-sort the acute, right and obtuse angles inside real triangles and quadrilaterals.
Keep mnemonics subordinate to meaning — 'a cute little angle' is a memory hook, not the definition, which is the comparison to a right angle.
keyRepresentations: The right-angle checker as the dividing benchmark, and an 'openness' scale from nothing to a straight line with the right angle marked in the middle
A hinge / fan sweeping through acute → right → obtuse
Overlay (vertex-on-vertex) comparison for ordering by opening
Acute / right / obtuse angles picked out and colour-sorted within shapes
commonMisconceptions: Ordering angles by arm length or by the distance between the tips rather than by the opening (Askew & Wiliam; Xu et al. list side length, enclosed area and distance between the sides as the irrelevant properties children use)
Judging by the space or area enclosed between the arms rather than the opening
Naming by appearance rather than by comparison to a right angle — a long-armed acute angle called obtuse because it 'looks big', or the two names simply swapped
Naming before comparing: applying acute/obtuse labels without checking against the right angle

learn.summary: Year 4 learners identify acute and obtuse angles and compare/order angles up to two right angles by size. Both names are anchored to the right angle: acute is less open than a right angle, obtuse is more open (but less than a straight line, i.e. two right angles). The persistent obstacle is comparing and ordering angles when the arm lengths differ — children tend to judge by arm length, enclosed area, or the distance between the tips rather than by the opening. The proposed core teaching move is vertex-on-vertex overlay comparison, with naming intended to follow secure less-than/greater-than-a-right-angle comparison rather than preceding it.

activities.title: Order the baited angles, then overlay to check
feedback: If a learner orders by arm length and places the long-armed narrow angle as largest, overlay that trapped pair vertex-on-vertex with one arm aligned so the narrow opening visibly folds inside the wide one; then re-sort by opening.
If a learner asks whether shortening the long arms would change its place, let them test it — shortening the arms does not change the opening, so the order stays the same.
Confirm correct orderings that are justified by comparing openings, overlaying, or relating each angle to a right angle, rather than by line length.
activities.rationale: A common comparison error is treating an angle as the distance between the ends of its lines, judging the angle with longer lines as larger; this may be reinforced when taught examples mostly use equal-length arms. Deliberately anti-correlating arm length with opening and then providing an overlay comparison is proposed to target exactly this misconception. An optional overlay tool that snaps two angles vertex-on-vertex, and a seeded four-angle task where the smallest opening has the longest arms, are intended to make the mechanism concrete.
sourceClaims: When comparing angles (from Year 3) the most common error is judging two identical angles as unequal because the arms differ in length, treating an angle as the distance between the ends of the lines; it arises because taught examples nearly always use equal-length arms.

When comparing angle size, elementary (and even middle-school) students are confused by irrelevant properties — the length of the sides, the area within the sides, and the distance between the sides — and mistakenly judge that the angle formed by longer lines is larger; this reflects a whole-object assumption, and framing angle as the measure of opening/rotation helps separate the size dimension.
Year 4 pupils should identify acute and obtuse angles and compare and order angles up to two right angles by size.
learnerActions: Receive four angles to drag into order from smallest to largest, where the smallest opening is deliberately drawn with the longest arms and the largest opening with the shortest arms.
State out loud, before moving anything, which angle you think is biggest and why.
Overlay any two angles vertex-on-vertex with one arm aligned, so only the openings are compared.

Overlay the longest-armed angle on the shortest-armed one and watch the long-armed 'big-looking' angle's opening fall INSIDE the short-armed angle's opening, then compare the other pairs the same way and re-sort all four by opening.
Re-state the rule you now use to decide the order.
activities.intendedInsight: An angle's size is its opening, not the length of its arms, the distance between the tips, or the area enclosed. Overlaying vertex-on-vertex with one arm aligned isolates the opening, so an angle with longer arms but a narrower opening is seen to be the smaller angle.

activities.title: Sweep a hinge through acute, right and obtuse
feedback: If a learner names an angle in a way that contradicts its comparison to a right angle, return to the checker: less open than a right angle is acute, more open (but less than a straight line) is obtuse — test before labelling.
Confirm that obtuse 'stops' at a straight line (two right angles); an angle that is exactly a straight line, or more open than one, is not obtuse.
Treat mnemonics such as 'a cute little angle' as a memory hook only, not the definition — the definition is the comparison to a right angle.
activities.rationale: A dynamic opening that sweeps continuously through the three named zones, with the right angle marked as the dividing benchmark, is intended to attach names to degrees of openness rather than to how a shape looks, supporting naming by comparison rather than by appearance. The live label and small-square snap-in are optional feedback examples that make the benchmark visible.
sourceClaims: Year 4 pupils should identify acute and obtuse angles and compare and order angles up to two right angles by size.

When comparing angle size, elementary (and even middle-school) students are confused by irrelevant properties — the length of the sides, the area within the sides, and the distance between the sides — and mistakenly judge that the angle formed by longer lines is larger; this reflects a whole-object assumption, and framing angle as the measure of opening/rotation helps separate the size dimension.
learnerActions: Open a hinge or fan slowly from nearly closed to a straight line.

Watch (or control) a label that ticks through acute → right → obtuse as the opening grows, with a small square snapping in at the right angle, and that changes to 'straight line (not obtuse)' when the opening reaches a straight line.
Pause the sweep and name the zone the opening is currently in.
Identify where obtuse stops — at a straight line, which equals two right angles.
activities.intendedInsight: The names acute, right and obtuse are zones of openness defined relative to the right-angle benchmark: acute is less open than a right angle, right is exactly a right angle, and obtuse is more open but less than a straight line (two right angles).

activities.title: Hunt and colour-sort angles inside shapes
feedback: If a learner labels an angle by appearance (e.g. calls a long-armed acute angle obtuse because it 'looks big'), return the naming to the checker and have them test the angle against a right angle before labelling.
Confirm classifications that are justified by comparison to the right angle rather than by overall size or orientation of the figure.
activities.rationale: Hunting for and colour-sorting the acute, right and obtuse angles inside triangles and convex quadrilaterals applies classification in a relational context — finding all angles of a type in a new shape — which is a more demanding application than classifying isolated angles. It is also intended to guard against naming by appearance when orientation or arm length is misleading.
sourceClaims: Year 4 pupils should identify acute and obtuse angles and compare and order angles up to two right angles by size.

When comparing angle size, elementary (and even middle-school) students are confused by irrelevant properties — the length of the sides, the area within the sides, and the distance between the sides — and mistakenly judge that the angle formed by longer lines is larger; this reflects a whole-object assumption, and framing angle as the measure of opening/rotation helps separate the size dimension.
learnerActions: Examine a given triangle or convex quadrilateral (one with no inside angle more open than a straight line).
Find every angle and decide whether it is acute, right or obtuse by comparing each to a right angle.
Colour-sort the angles by type (e.g. one colour for acute, one for right, one for obtuse).
Explain, for a tricky angle, how you checked it against the right angle rather than guessing from its appearance.
activities.intendedInsight: Acute, right and obtuse angles occur inside real shapes, and each is classified by comparison to a right angle — not by the orientation of the shape or the length of its sides.

activities.title: Predict-then-check: short wide angle vs long narrow angle
feedback: If a learner predicts the long-armed angle is bigger because of its line lengths, overlay the pair vertex-on-vertex with one arm aligned so the narrow opening folds inside the wide one, then relate each back to the right-angle benchmark.

If a learner judges by the gap between the tips or the enclosed space, mark an arc at the vertex and slide it in and out along the arms to show the opening is the same however far out you look; then overlay to compare the opening alone, ignoring the shaded region.
Confirm answers that order by opening and justify by overlaying or comparing to a right angle, not by line length.
activities.rationale: Asking for a prediction and a reason before any movement is intended to surface whether the learner is using the length rule or comparing openings; the overlay then provides the disconfirming evidence. Marking and sliding an arc at the vertex addresses the related area/tip-distance misconception by showing the opening is invariant to how far out along the arms you look.
sourceClaims: When comparing angles (from Year 3) the most common error is judging two identical angles as unequal because the arms differ in length, treating an angle as the distance between the ends of the lines; it arises because taught examples nearly always use equal-length arms.

When comparing angle size, elementary (and even middle-school) students are confused by irrelevant properties — the length of the sides, the area within the sides, and the distance between the sides — and mistakenly judge that the angle formed by longer lines is larger; this reflects a whole-object assumption, and framing angle as the measure of opening/rotation helps separate the size dimension.
learnerActions: Look at two angles: A with short arms and a wide opening, B with long arms and a narrow opening.
Predict which is the bigger angle and say why, before anything is moved.
Overlay them vertex-on-vertex with one arm aligned so B's second arm falls inside A's.
Reconcile your prediction with what the overlay shows, and restate the rule for comparing angles.
Answer the probe: if the long arms were made much shorter, would the angle's place in the order change? Why? And could a short-armed angle ever be bigger than a long-armed one — can you draw one?
activities.intendedInsight: The reason a learner gives first is the diagnostic part: a learner who predicts B is bigger 'because its lines are longer' is asked to reconcile that with the wider opening of A winning once the angles are overlaid.

constraints: Anchor both names to the right angle: compare every angle to a right-angle checker before naming it. Acute = less open than a right angle; obtuse = more open but less than a straight line (two right angles).

Order by superimposing openings, not by eyeballing the tips: overlay angles vertex-on-vertex with one arm aligned so only the opening is compared. Because the overlay compares the openings alone, differences in arm length, enclosed area and tip distance cannot drive the comparison.
Naming should follow secure less-than/greater-than-a-right-angle comparison, not precede it.
Keep mnemonics subordinate to meaning — 'a cute little angle' is a memory hook, not the definition.

A static picture that reveals labels when tapped supports recognition and classification of clear cases, but it cannot carry out the overlay comparison or the dynamic sweep; treat it as a scaffold for classification only, not a replacement for the overlay work.

Classification and ordering practice (classifying angles as acute/right/obtuse, ordering them by size, and finding all of a type in a shape) is useful for assessment and practice, but recognising and ordering angles does not by itself build the overlay intuition for the length trap; pair it with hands-on overlay work.

If learners manipulate physical paper/card angle cutouts, note that cutouts have slight real thickness and can be held and overlaid, whereas the on-screen or ideal figure is a zero-thickness model of the mathematical angle; the comparison is about the represented angle, not the physical card.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The legacy row rated 3D and in-role dialogue formats as poor fits and asserted a static image cannot build overlay intuition. These are presented here as narrowly scoped affordance/limit observations (a static reveal cannot perform the dynamic overlay or live sweep), not as universal claims about what any medium can teach; the cited sources establish the misconception and curriculum content, not comparative efficacy between media.

Self-audit of the geometry: an angle's measure is its opening and is invariant to arm length and to how far out along the arms you look; the 'slide the arc in and out' demonstration is consistent with this. Obtuse angles are those strictly between a right angle and a straight line; a straight line (two right angles) is the upper bound for this Year 4 topic. No arithmetic or force/motion content was present to correct.

The legacy attribution of this four-angle ordering task as 'Askew & Wiliam's documented diagnostic task' and the phrase that the overlay 'defeats' the trap have been softened to proposed/geometric wording; the sources support the misconception's prevalence and the curriculum objective but not comparative efficacy of this specific design.

The colour-sort method itself is not evidenced by the cited sources; its supporting claims cover the identify-acute/obtuse content and the appearance-naming misconception it addresses, not the recolouring technique's effectiveness.

assess.poeTask: Show two angles: A with short arms and a wide opening, B with long arms and a narrow opening. Ask the child to PREDICT which is the bigger angle and WHY before anything is moved. Then overlay them vertex-on-vertex with one arm aligned so B's second arm falls inside A's. A child who predicted B 'because its lines are longer' must confront the wider opening winning; the reason stated first is the diagnostic part.
probeDeeper: You put this one first as the smallest, and it has the longest lines. If I made its lines much shorter, would it change its place in the order? Why?
Show me how you'd check, without measuring, whether this angle is acute or obtuse.
Is it possible for an angle with short little lines to be bigger than an angle with long lines? Can you draw me one?
How open can an angle get and still be called obtuse — where does obtuse stop?
assess.correctAnswer: Orders the angles by their opening, ignoring arm length (so the long-armed narrow angle goes first and the short-armed wide angle last), and justifies by comparing openings, overlaying, or relating each to a right angle — not by how long the lines are.

errorPatterns.pattern: The angle with the longest lines is the biggest ('longer arms mean a bigger angle')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Overlay the trapped pair vertex-on-vertex with one arm aligned so the narrow opening visibly folds inside the wide one; re-sort by opening and return to the right-angle benchmark.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Orders by arm length, placing the long-armed narrow-opening angle as the largest, and justifies by mentioning the line lengths

errorPatterns.pattern: Judges by the space or gap between the arms — the angle that encloses more area, or whose tips are further apart, is the bigger angle
errorPatterns.nextMove: Mark the arc at the vertex and slide it in and out along the arms to show the opening is the same however far out you look; overlay to compare opening alone, ignoring the shaded region.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Ranks a short-armed wide angle below a long-armed narrow one because it 'takes up less space' or its tips are closer together

errorPatterns.pattern: Names by appearance, not by comparison to a right angle — a long-armed acute angle called obtuse because it 'looks big', or acute and obtuse swapped
errorPatterns.nextMove: Return every naming to the checker — less open than a right angle is acute, more open is obtuse — and have the child test before labelling.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Labels an angle acute or obtuse in a way that contradicts its comparison to a right angle, especially when arm length or orientation is misleading

responseLevels.gap: Orders and names angles by arm length, tip-distance, or enclosed space; swaps acute and obtuse or names by appearance; cannot separate the opening from the overall figure.
responseLevels.full: Orders and classifies purely by opening — overlaying or comparing to a right angle regardless of arm length — explains acute as less and obtuse as more open than a right angle (up to a straight line / two right angles), and finds all the acute and obtuse angles in a new shape (relational).
responseLevels.partial: Classifies clear acute / right / obtuse cases and recalls the names, and orders angles correctly when the arms are the same length, but is misled when arm length is anti-correlated with opening, or names an angle without comparing it to a right angle (multistructural).

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Give the child four angles to order from smallest to largest, with arm length deliberately anti-correlated with opening — the smallest opening is drawn with the longest arms and the largest opening with the shortest arms. Say: 'Put these four angles in order, from the smallest angle to the biggest.' Then: 'Tell me how you decided the order.'
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Anti-correlating arm length with opening means a child using the length rule produces a specifically reversed order on the trapped pair, while a child comparing openings orders correctly; the tier-2 reason reveals which method was used. This is Askew & Wiliam's documented diagnostic task for the misconception.
